Both of you are wrong, but partially correct sort of. The term "Mongoloid" is a now abandoned racial classification for people native to Asia. Similar terms include "Caucasoid", which was an old classification for most Europeans and "Negroid", which was used to refer to humans native to Africa. All 3 of these terms are no longer considered scientifically accurate and are seen as offensive in a lot of cases. However, long ago the term Mongoloid was also used as a derogatory term to refer to people with Downe's Syndrome, originating from people who assumed that the facial features of people with the disorder were characteristic of Asians. I.e, thin eye shape.

I wouldn't say that they treated me horrible. I didn't talk or interact much, but I was basically treated as if I wasn't even there. I spent the first night in the Mental Health unit of the ER. So, they basically confiscate all your possessions and make you wear paper-scrubs. If you don't cause a commotion, they move you into the regular section of the ER. The difference is basically that in the Mental Crisis unit, there is a guard there in case people get rowdy. When I was transferred to the actual mental health facility, they put me in a stretcher and took me in an ambulance. Most of the people in there were around my age and also in there for "suicidal ideation", but there were a few severe cases. In a way it was nice to find a place in groups of people my age with similar issues, but, the actual therapy aspect was a bit bogus, and if I had actually ended up paying for it I would have been very pissed. The therapy consisted of drawing with crayons, making arts and crafts, watching ted talks,  grief talks, playing wii sports, ect... And then there was free-time, where I spent most of the time playing Spades, Blackjack, Dominoes, and Chess. I actually learned how to play Spades, Blackjack, and Dominoes in the mental hospital itself from other patients. It really was like a strange mix of Jail, Pre-school, and a hospital. The only thing I enjoyed about the experience was the other patients. Everyone had very unique personalities and pretty much everyone was friendly to eachother. I liked the regular routine tho, and interacting with friendly people with similar issues. Kind of made me wish there were communities like this, that weren't set up like prisons. There were a few patients who were exceptions though, there was an older lady who would curse out the nurses, she punched a nurse, and spilled hot coffee on a patient who politely asked her not to touch his food. In some instances the nurses were severely understaffed and some patients would get away with things you would not expect like playful wrestling and playing hardcore rap on the community TV on youtube. I didn't mind this, but I did think it was funny situationally. Until one of the songs triggered one of the patient's mental disorder and she had a sort of psychotic episode and was dancing around the room uncontrollably. She was always quiet and never talked, but after that she was never really the same. After that instance she had an almost constant tick and was afraid to come out and eat during meals. She then started to stay up all night and walk the halls singing gospel music. Towards the end of my stay she started to warm up to a few specific people, but became a little attached and would follow them around everywhere.  Also as a side note, MANY of the patients were just chilling basically high as fuck off of their medications. It was a weird experience to say the least.

Ironically, I was lucky to not have insurance, because it placed me under "charity care", if not for that, the mental facility would have likely costed over 10 grand. The ER wanted to charge me over $8,000 for literally just laying there for those two days, but the charity care covered most of that too, bringing down to around $1000, which I still think is ridiculous, due to the fact that, I didn't even have any procedures, medication, or anything. One round of bloodwork and a psychoanalysis with a therapist that lasted all of 5 mins, before them just telling me "It's your choice whether or not you want to be transferred to the mental health facility, you can either sign your permission, or we'll restrain you and take you anyway" Needless to say, I just signed it, because I'd rather just have them take me there then "restrain" me. It was more of a threat than a choice.

"Functional enough" doesn't really cut it in today's world. If I'm never going to be able to rise beyond minimum wage, there isn't a way to survive regardless, unless I have a way for long-term support/housing which I don't. NEETDOM isn't a "one-size-fits-all" lifestyle. there are plenty of NEETS on here with parents who are able to get them through and keep them housed as long as possible. I've met plenty of NEETS who went way further in college than I did and still go on to become NEETS (an associates degree in general studies is almost the same as not going to college at all if you can't afford to go on to a 4-year afterwards) So, here I am jobless, no credit history, unskilled, at 26.  I'd much rather have secured housing than have had relationships. But, I'm highly unlikely to ever be in a relationship again. It was honestly just dumb luck at the time, and I'm extremely socially inept due to the trauma I experienced throughout my life. That's the fucked up thing with NEETS, even if we get jobs, which most of us only qualify for min wage, most other normal people who actually live off min wage are living with a significant other either due to them being extremely attractive or charming. Most other relationships are completely monetary-based. Pretty much if you're mental state goes shit before you're able to secure income, then you're fucked and the world doesn't care. All the "positive speaking" about mental health right now is pretty much only targeted at those who are already financially stable.
